name: trim-my-output
summary: Terse caveman-voice replies that keep every technical fact, code, path and number verbatim; stays on until "stop caveman" or "normal mode".
when: The user types /caveman or says "caveman mode", "be brief" or "less tokens"
Every output token is billed and read in a terminal
The answer needs to lead with the result, with ceremony and hedging removed
A long session should stay compressed until the user says "normal mode"
Routine tool runs need one-line status instead of narration
notWhen: A security warning or irreversible action is involved; break the rules and use plain prose, confirming in full sentences first
Anything persisted outside chat (code, comments, commits, docs, issues, PRs, tickets, memory files) must stay plain
Step order could be scrambled by a fragment, or the user is confused or repeating the question
The user asks for /caveman ultra or /caveman wenyan; those route to the ultracave or megacave skill
example: "/caveman" → the agent answers first in terse plain sentences, keeping code, paths, numbers and errors verbatim.

gate.what: Irreversible actions require confirming in full sentences before proceeding, and security warnings drop the terseness.

name: write-less-code
summary: Lazy senior dev mode: smallest complete change that solves the task, shortest working diff, no unrequested abstraction, plus a reply a busy human reads once.
when: Any coding task: writing, fixing, refactoring, reviewing, choosing dependencies
The user says ponytail, be lazy, simplest solution, or yagni
The user complains about over-engineering or bloat
A vague build request needs the smallest version that does the core job
Deciding whether a new dependency or abstraction is warranted
notWhen: Being smaller would mean cutting validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, or something the user asked for
The user explicitly wants options, flexibility, or extensibility nobody has asked to skip
The work is a spec, plan, or prose document rather than a coding change
example: "/write-less-code add retry to the upload call" → the agent greps callers, reuses the existing retry helper, and changes one call site.

gate.what: Ultra level pushes back on the request before building, but no destructive action needs approval.

name: route-to-the-right-skill
summary: The parent skill. Every other skill is a phase it routes to: check for an applicable skill before you act, say which one you are using, and re-route when the phase changes, two attempts fail, the scope moves, or you are about to claim done.
when: Starting a session, before the first tool call
Crossing a phase boundary: spec approved, review passed, tests green
Two attempts on the same problem have failed, so it is a debug problem now
The user changes what they want and the spec is stale
About to say done, fixed or works
About to run a destructive or scope-expanding command
Unsure which of the 42 skills applies, or whether any does
notWhen: Never skip it: the check is compulsory even when its conclusion is that no skill applies
It is not the work itself. If it is the only skill you used, you routed and never arrived
Not a substitute for reading the skill it names: routing without reading is the failure it exists to prevent
example: "Fix the login redirect bug" → the agent checks for a skill, names the phase (Debug), says "Using debug-this-code", reads that file, and re-checks once the fix lands, which is Verify → prove-it-works.

gate.what: No approval gate of its own. It hands you to the skill that has one: guard-the-dangerous-stuff before a destructive command, review-the-plan before code.

name: interview-me-properly
summary: Interviews the user one question at a time, each with a guess, until ~95% confidence, then restates intent for an explicit yes.
when: The ask is missing who, why, what success looks like, or the binding constraint
The request is conventional ("build me X", "make it faster") and needs unpacking
The user says interview me, grill me, or stress-test my thinking
You catch yourself about to fill in ambiguous requirements before any plan, spec or code
notWhen: The ask is unambiguous and self-contained (rename a variable, fix a typo)
The user explicitly asked for speed over verification
Pure information requests such as how does X work, or mechanical renames, formats and file moves
Non-interactive contexts: CI pipelines, scheduled runs, /loop, autonomous loops
example: "/interview-me-properly build me a dashboard" → the agent states a one-sentence hypothesis with a confidence number, then asks one question with its guess attached.

gate.what: No destructive action, but it requires an explicit yes on the restated intent before any spec, plan or downstream tool call.

name: discuss-on-new-idea
summary: Refines a vague idea through divergent variations, convergent assumption stress-testing, and a one-pager with an explicit Not Doing list.
when: Idea is still vague and needs shaping before it can become a plan
You want options expanded before converging on one
You want assumptions attacked before they become a plan
User says ideate, refine this idea, or stress-test my plan
A one-pager with MVP scope and a Not Doing list is the deliverable
notWhen: The user is unsure what they want at all — use interview-me
A direction is already chosen and needs a spec — use spec-driven-development
The task is fixing existing behaviour rather than shaping a new idea
example: "Help me refine this idea: an internal wiki" → the agent restates it as a How Might We, asks 3-5 sharpening questions, then proposes variations.

gate.what: Nothing destructive is gated.

name: research-this-topic
summary: Researches a question against official primary sources and writes cited findings to a Markdown file, with a background agent doing the reading.
when: The user wants a topic researched, or docs and API facts gathered
You are about to write framework-specific code from memory
The user wants reading legwork delegated to a background agent
A pattern must be confirmed against the exact pinned version
The user asks for documented, verified, or "correct" implementation
notWhen: Correctness does not depend on version — renames, typo fixes, moving files
Pure logic identical across all versions — loops, conditionals, data structures
The user explicitly wants speed over verification ("just do it quickly")
You cannot fetch sources and would answer from training data anyway
example: "Research React 19 form handling and write it up" → the agent detects versions in package.json, then fetches react.dev pages.

gate.what: Stopping points are questions on ambiguous versions or doc-versus-code conflicts; writing the findings file is not destructive.

name: explore-this-repo
summary: Read-only explorer that fans out broad searches and returns only path:line citations of where relevant code lives, keeping reads out of main context.
when: Cold-start orientation in an unfamiliar repo
Broad cross-file localization across many files
A direct search already failed
You need to know where code lives, not have it changed
Delegating localization so the reads stay out of main context
notWhen: The exact file or symbol is already named
You want an edit or a proposed solution — this agent never edits, runs commands, or proposes fixes
You already know the path and just need the file read
example: "Where does model routing happen?" → the agent fires parallel Glob, Grep and Read calls, then replies with only path:line citations.

gate.what: Read-only; nothing destructive is gated.

name: write-the-spec
summary: Turns intent into a gated, executable spec covering objectives, commands, structure, code style, testing, boundaries and success criteria before any code is written.
when: Starting a new project or feature
Requirements are ambiguous or incomplete
The change touches multiple files or modules
You are about to make an architectural decision
The task would take more than 30 minutes to implement
One request bundles several independently testable capabilities and needs a capability map first
notWhen: Single-line fixes, typo corrections, or changes that are unambiguous and self-contained
A spec already exists and you need to slice it into tasks; planning-and-task-breakdown owns that
The work is already coded and only needs documentation
example: "/write-the-spec add team billing" → the agent first lists its assumptions, then asks clarifying questions before writing the spec file.

gate.what: After saving the spec the agent must end its turn and get human approval before any planning or code.

name: write-the-domain-glossary
summary: Sharpens a project's domain model: challenges terms, records them in GLOSSARY.md, offers ADRs for hard-to-reverse decisions, and reviews the prose.
when: Discussing or challenging codebase terminology
Writing or editing a GLOSSARY.md
Recording an architecture decision as an ADR
The user's term conflicts with the existing glossary definition
The user uses vague or overloaded terms that need one canonical term
Domain relationships need stress-testing with concrete scenarios
notWhen: Merely reading GLOSSARY.md to pick up vocabulary; that is a one-line habit, not this skill
The decision is easy to reverse, unsurprising without context, or involved no real trade-off: skip the ADR
You need to store specs, scratch notes, or implementation details; GLOSSARY.md must hold none of those
example: The user says "account" → the agent asks whether that means the Customer or the User, then writes the resolved term into GLOSSARY.md.

gate.what: It calls out conflicts inline and only offers ADRs, with no approval gate on a destructive action.

name: document-the-decision
summary: Records the why behind decisions as ADRs, API docs, README and changelog, matching existing project convention before its own template.
when: A significant architectural decision needs its rationale written
Choosing between competing approaches
Adding or changing a public API
Shipping a feature that changes user-facing behaviour
You keep explaining the same decision repeatedly
notWhen: Documenting obvious code or restating what the code already says
Throwaway prototypes
Leaving TODO comments or commented-out code instead of doing or deleting it
example: "Document the decision to use PostgreSQL" → the agent inspects the existing ADR convention, then writes context, alternatives and consequences.

gate.what: Documentation-only; nothing destructive is gated.

name: break-into-tasks
summary: Decomposes an approved plan into thin vertical slices with demo lines and dependency order in M###-ROADMAP.md, or GitHub issues after confirmation.
when: break this into slices
decompose the plan
vertical slices
break into issues
the roadmap's slices are too thick, too few or badly ordered
notWhen: Scope is not signed off yet; it runs only once M###-CONTEXT.md is stable
The deliverable is a document or a spike rather than working code, which it explicitly calls not-a-slice
You want GitHub issues filed automatically — that needs explicit confirmation every time
example: "/break-into-tasks on the checkout milestone" → the agent reads M###-CONTEXT.md and the codebase seams, drafts vertical slices with risk and depends, then asks about granularity.

gate.what: Filing GitHub issues (outward, irreversible) needs explicit confirmation, and M###-ROADMAP.md is only written after the user approves the breakdown.

name: review-the-plan
summary: Adversarially reviews a plan or design as junior work, grounds findings in codebase and current sources, then writes a promoted rewrite.
when: A plan is ready for sign-off
You want the assumptions attacked before they become code
A design needs a harder look than its author can give it
An agent-generated plan is fog (no interfaces) or tunnel (no product vision)
The plan's factual claims need checking against the actual repo
notWhen: The code is already written and only the diff needs reviewing — use review-my-code
No plan artifact exists yet — the skill says do not review thin air
A one-line fix or typo with no design decisions behind it
You need a product direction decided — the skill refuses to invent one
example: "/review-the-plan on the caching plan I just wrote" → the agent freezes the artifact, extracts 2-5 domains, then researches the codebase and current docs.

gate.what: It produces a review plus rewrite and surfaces product decisions as open questions; it never applies the rewrite silently.

name: design-the-interface
summary: Produces several radically different interface designs, compares them on depth and seam placement, then synthesizes and records a recommendation.
when: Asked to design an interface or shape an API
Planning a new deep module where the first idea is unlikely to be best
Exploring module boundaries and where the seam belongs
Choosing between competing interface shapes
Before writing implementation for a public API
notWhen: The work is implementation detail — file paths, call graphs, internal data structures (implementation creep)
You want a build-effort ranking; "easiest to build" is explicitly not an interface argument
Nothing actually varies across the seam — one adapter means a hypothetical seam
example: "Design the interface for our repo storage layer" → the agent drafts three genuinely different shapes, each with a usage example, before comparing.

gate.what: Design-only; nothing destructive is gated.

name: isolate-this-branch
summary: Creates an isolated git worktree through a native tool or git fallback, then installs dependencies and verifies a clean test baseline.
when: Starting feature work that must be isolated from the current workspace
Before executing an implementation plan
You may already be in a worktree or submodule and need Step 0 detection
You need a verified clean test baseline before implementing
notWhen: You are already in a linked worktree — the skill says do not create another
The user declined worktree consent — work in place instead
You are inside a submodule — treat it as a normal repo, not a worktree
The sandbox denied git worktree add — fall back to working in the current directory
example: "/isolate-this-branch start the auth refactor in a worktree" → the agent runs Step 0 detection, asks consent, then creates the worktree.

gate.what: It asks consent before creating a worktree and asks the human whether to proceed when baseline tests fail.

name: build-it-test-first
summary: Drives changes with a red-green-refactor test loop and reproduces every bug in a failing test before fixing it.
when: Implementing any new logic or behavior
A bug report arrives
Modifying existing functionality
Adding edge case handling
Asked to add tests to a function that has none
notWhen: Pure configuration changes
Documentation, static content or other updates with no behavioral impact — its own stated exclusions
example: "Fix this bug: completedAt is never set" → the agent writes a failing test that reproduces the missing timestamp, runs the repo's test command, then makes the minimal fix.

gate.what: No approval gate; it writes the failing test, fixes, and runs the full suite autonomously.

name: build-in-small-steps
summary: Implements a change in thin vertical slices, testing, verifying and committing each one before starting the next.
when: Implementing any multi-file change
Building a new feature from a task breakdown
Refactoring existing code
You are about to write more than ~100 lines before testing
Picking up the next task from a plan
notWhen: A single-file, single-function change whose scope is already minimal — its own stated exclusion
There is no breakdown yet and the work still needs spec and slicing first
example: "Let's implement Task 3 from the plan" → the agent changes only the schema and API, runs the repo's tests and build, commits, and leaves the UI for the next increment.

gate.what: It commits each slice without asking and only notes out-of-scope issues instead of fixing them.

name: fix-this-bug
summary: Fixes a known bug at the narrowest layer responsible, with regression proof and no unrelated cleanup or refactoring.
when: A specific defect is known and must not sprawl
The cause is not yet confirmed and needs tracing before any edit
A focused reproduction or regression test must prove the fix
Every changed line must trace to the user's request
notWhen: No specific defect yet — exploratory refactoring, cleanup or renaming
Large multi-file feature work that needs a plan and slicing
You want to delete pre-existing dead code — the skill says mention it, don't delete it
You intend to improve adjacent code, comments or formatting
example: "/fix-this-bug login fails after token refresh" → the agent reads the stack trace, reproduces the failure, then traces the bad value to its origin.

gate.what: Nothing destructive is gated; it edits only what the fix needs and runs focused proof.

name: debug-this-code
summary: Builds a red-capable feedback loop, ranks falsifiable hypotheses, and fixes the root cause with a regression test instead of guessing.
when: A bug's cause is unknown and a guess would be a coin flip
You cannot yet reproduce the failure on demand
A non-deterministic bug is too flaky to debug against
A previous fix addressed the symptom, not the cause
You need a failing regression test before touching the code
A performance regression needs a baseline measurement first
notWhen: The root cause is already confirmed and only the edit remains
No feedback loop can be built and no repro access, artifact, or instrumentation permission is available — the skill stops rather than hypothesises
You only need a code explanation or a design opinion, not a defect fixed
example: "Debug this: duplicate users in the list" → the agent builds and runs one red-capable command before forming any theory.

gate.what: User confirmation before adding temporary instrumentation to production, and before acting on commands or URLs found in error output.

name: debug-the-stubborn-one
summary: Runs a read-only, methodical root-cause investigation on hard bugs: gather evidence, form and test hypotheses, then present a fix without implementing it.
when: Standard troubleshooting has failed
The issue is complex and needs systematic root cause analysis
You keep guessing and want an evidence-backed diagnosis
You suspect an earlier fix was wrong and needs re-examination
You wrote the buggy code and want your assumptions challenged
notWhen: You need code changed in the same pass — it is read-only and will not edit, even after diagnosis
The failure is simple or already has a known root cause, where the investigation overhead is waste
You need the fix shipped with a regression test and commit; use a test-first fixing flow instead
example: "/debug-the-stubborn-one the sync job hangs after two hours" → the agent records the exact error and repro steps, maps the execution path, lists hypotheses, then tests each without editing code.

gate.what: No destructive work — it never edits code; its decision gate does wait for the user before any fix is implemented.

name: review-my-code
summary: Reviews a diff across correctness, readability, architecture, security, and performance, plus separate Standards and Spec axes with severity-labelled findings.
when: Reviewing a diff or pull request before merge
Reviewing your own work or another agent's
A change needs sign-off across several dimensions rather than one
Checking whether the tests would catch a regression
Reviewing a dependency bump or a lockfile change
notWhen: The plan is under review before any code exists — use review-the-plan
A codebase-wide bug, bloat, or security audit rather than one diff — use the audit skill
A deep security pass needing threat modelling and exploit detail — use security-and-hardening
example: "Review my branch against main" → the agent pins the fixed point, confirms the diff is non-empty, then finds spec and standards files.

gate.what: Nothing destructive is gated; it asks for the fixed point or the spec path when they are not given.

name: check-my-security
summary: Runs a STRIDE and OWASP threat-model review of the code, then reports each finding with a concrete exploit, severity and remediation.
when: Before shipping anything that touches auth, input handling, secrets or data storage
Review this for security
Is this login flow safe
We added file uploads, CORS or a new external integration
Check dependency and supply-chain risk via the native audit
notWhen: The change touches no auth, input handling, secrets or stored data, so there is no trust boundary to review
You want the whole repo audited for bugs, load and bloat rather than security alone
You want forced dependency remediation applied for you — it never runs npm audit fix --force automatically
example: "/check-my-security on the new upload endpoint" → the agent maps trust boundaries, walks STRIDE and the OWASP checklist over the actual code, then triages findings by severity x exploitability.

gate.what: Adding auth flows, storing new PII, changing CORS, adding upload handlers, altering rate limits or granting roles needs human approval; findings stay private until the user agrees to file them.

name: receive-code-review
summary: Handles incoming code review feedback with verification and technical pushback instead of performative agreement, clarifying unclear items before implementing.
when: Review feedback has arrived and you are about to implement it
Some feedback items are unclear or seem technically questionable
An external reviewer made a suggestion you cannot easily verify
Multi-item feedback such as "fix 1-6"
A reviewer asks to "implement properly" something you suspect is unused
notWhen: You are the one writing the review — that is review-my-code
No feedback exists yet; this is new code with no reviewer
The request is a product or architecture direction that belongs to the human partner — the skill says stop and discuss, not implement
example: "Reviewer says remove the legacy compat shim" → the agent checks the codebase for real callers before editing anything.

gate.what: It halts and asks before implementing anything when any feedback item is unclear or conflicts with the human partner's prior decisions.

name: audit-the-whole-repo
summary: Audits a whole repo for bugs, security holes, load failures, untested risky code, slowness and bloat, then returns a ranked plain-English report without changing code.
when: Audit this codebase
Review the whole repo
Find bloat
What can I delete
You inherited a repo and need to know what is wrong with it
notWhen: You want something changed: it is a one-shot report and changes no code
The scope is one diff or pull request, not a folder, package or repo
You need real load or profiling evidence; this only judges the expected load from the code and says which load it assumed
example: "Audit this repo before I take it over" → the agent reads README, build config, dependencies, entry points and tests, states the assumed load, then traces the main data flows.

gate.what: Read-only: it greps whole-tree references, reads files and reports, but never edits or deletes code.

name: prove-it-works
summary: Blocks any claim that work is complete, fixed, or passing until a fresh verification command has been run and its output read.
when: About to claim tests pass, a bug is fixed, or a build succeeds
About to commit, push, or open a PR
About to move to the next task
A subagent or agent reports success
You catch yourself writing "should", "probably", or "seems to"
notWhen: No status claim is being made — a question, a read, or a design discussion
No verification command exists for the claim, so there is nothing fresh to run and the limitation must be stated instead
Relying on a partial check, a previous run, or a linter in place of the compiler
example: "Is the fix done?" → the agent runs the full test command, reads exit code and failure count, then answers.

gate.what: It is a self-imposed evidence gate before claims; it asks no one for approval.

name: test-every-surface
summary: Report-only QA for API, CLI, job, worker and webhook surfaces: isolated fixtures, a contract map, retained evidence and a reproducible report. Never fixes bugs.
when: Testing an HTTP API, CLI, job, worker or webhook rather than a browser UI
Coverage must include invalid input, auth, exit codes, timeouts, retries, idempotency or partial failure
On a feature branch without explicit scope, using diff-aware testing of changed and adjacent behavior
Replaying a prior functional report in regression mode
A reproducible evidence report is required, with findings separated from hypotheses
notWhen: Browser flows: the description routes those to check-my-ui
You want the bug fixed or product tests written; this run never edits product code, tests, config or tracked state
Production access, destruction or external mutation without permission naming the target, operation and effect
A browser target has no documented test framework; report the gap instead of installing anything
example: "/test-every-surface the checkout API" → the agent selects the functional surface, sets up isolated fixtures and announces target, tools and permitted writes.

gate.what: Production access, destruction or external mutation needs explicit permission naming the target, operation and effect; unknown ownership blocks the probe.

name: check-my-ui
summary: Drives a real browser to open the page, click the flow, screenshot it and inspect DOM, console, network and performance.
when: Building or debugging anything that runs in a browser
Before shipping a change with a visible surface
A UI bug needs reproducing in a real browser
Console errors or failed network requests need checking
Page load, layout shift or interaction performance needs measuring
notWhen: The problem lives in a CLI, job, worker, webhook or API with no browser surface
The behaviour is pure logic that a unit test covers faster
You need the source code changed: this is a see-and-verify pass, not an implementation skill
example: "Check the checkout page after my CSS change" → the agent opens it in its own tab, screenshots before and after, clicks the flow and inspects console, network and accessibility.

gate.what: On a non-local site any mutating action (submit, create, delete, purchase, change settings) needs explicit consent once per run before the first one.

name: make-it-accessible
summary: Audits and fixes web accessibility to WCAG 2.1: alt text, contrast, keyboard paths, focus, labels, motion and ARIA.
when: Running an a11y audit or WCAG 2.1 compliance pass
Keyboard navigation, focus order or visible focus problems
Screen-reader semantics, form labels or colour contrast are wrong
Before shipping any user-facing surface
notWhen: Non-web UI with no HTML/CSS or ARIA surface — the guidance targets web pages and components
Nothing user-facing changes, e.g. a backend-only edit
You only want an automated Lighthouse/axe score — the skill still requires manual keyboard, screen-reader, zoom and reduced-motion checks
Reference-led design where you plan to copy another product's branding, text, imagery or exact layout — the skill forbids it
example: "/make-it-accessible audit the signup form for WCAG 2.1" → the agent checks labels, alt text, contrast, keyboard path and focus order first.

gate.what: Nothing destructive or irreversible; it edits markup, CSS and JS without an approval gate.

name: finish-the-experience
summary: Finds and finishes the experiential last 20%: the magic moment, page shapes, empty states and defaults, before a build is called done.
when: Planning a build so the magic is specced as concretely as the plumbing
The solution works but feels like a demo
User says last 20%, finish this, make it actually good, is this done
The output reads like filler, or the first run feels dead
Before declaring any build done
notWhen: Adding features — the last 20% is depth on the core scene, never breadth
Rewriting working infrastructure to be prettier inside (gold-plating the plumbing)
The walk already delivers the magic moment — a solution is allowed to pass
example: "Is this wiki actually done?" → the agent writes the magic-moment scene and scene list, then walks the wiki cold as a first-time user.

gate.what: Nothing destructive is gated.

name: polish-the-ui
summary: Builds and polishes accessible, responsive UI: component structure, state, design tokens, typography, colour, motion, and WCAG 2.1 AA checks before delivery.
when: Building new UI components or pages
Modifying existing user-facing interfaces
Implementing responsive layouts
Adding interactivity or state management
Fixing visual or UX issues
The output must not look AI-generated
notWhen: No rendered surface at all — backend, API, CLI, or data-layer work
Copying another product's branding, proprietary text, imagery, or exact layout — the skill forbids it
Colour, spacing, or type decisions already fixed by a DESIGN.md token spec you were told to follow verbatim
example: "/polish-the-ui the settings page looks AI-generated" → the agent first collects 2-3 reference screens and writes a short design contract.

gate.what: It edits UI code and defers to an existing DESIGN.md; nothing destructive or irreversible.

name: landing-page-design
summary: Builds a high-conversion landing page: intake, page structure, layout, conversion copy, SEO, and a strict visual system for type, spacing, radius, colour, icons and motion.
when: Building a landing page or marketing site from scratch
Choosing page sections, headlines, CTAs or a layout
Writing or reviewing conversion copy for one offer and one audience
Setting type, spacing, radius and colour values for a page
Reviewing a landing page before it ships
notWhen: Upgrading an existing site rather than building one — the upstream project ships a separate redesign skill
Backend, API, CLI or data-layer work with no rendered page
A DESIGN.md already fixes every visual value you were told to follow verbatim
Copying another product's branding, proprietary text, imagery or exact layout
example: "/landing-page-design build the waitlist page for our beta" → the agent asks for the one action, audience and offer before choosing any section or type value.

gate.what: It writes page code and copy; nothing destructive or irreversible.

name: design-to-motion
summary: Turns a static design into a pixel-exact animated HTML replica that loads from an empty state and loops every visual's story, then exports an MP4 and GIFs.
when: Animating a Figma frame, screenshot, dashboard, card set or hero image
Making a loading, appear or showcase loop for a design
Building a motion mockup, video or GIF of a design
Adding bento or feature cards that pair text with a visual on a site
notWhen: Shipping interaction motion inside a product such as hovers, menus or toasts — use polish-the-ui
The job is a checked diagram, not an animated design — use diagram-the-system
A redesign is wanted rather than a faithful animation of the existing frame
A Figma token, headless Chrome or ffmpeg is unavailable and exports are required
example: "/design-to-motion animate this Figma frame for X" → the agent rebuilds the exact frame, defines the story loops, then records and encodes the MP4 and GIF.

gate.what: It writes HTML, frames and media files and runs ffmpeg; nothing destructive or irreversible.

name: make-it-fast
summary: Measures first, fixes only the measured bottleneck, re-measures to keep or revert, then guards the metric against regression.
when: Performance requirements exist: load-time budgets or response-time SLAs
Users or monitoring report slow behavior
Core Web Vitals are below thresholds
You suspect a change introduced a performance regression
N+1 queries or index problems show up in the query log
notWhen: There is no evidence of a problem yet — premature optimization adds complexity for nothing
The re-measured gain sits inside run-to-run noise — that is a revert, not a keep
The win requires changing, skipping or deleting a test to land
You plan to raise the connection pool without finding what holds connections
example: "/make-it-fast checkout LCP is 4.2s" → the agent captures a Lighthouse baseline, profiles the waterfall, and fixes only the largest bottleneck.

gate.what: Nothing destructive or irreversible; it profiles, edits, and reverts unproven changes itself.

name: make-it-observable
summary: Instruments production code with structured logs, RED/USE metrics, OpenTelemetry traces and symptom-based alerts so incidents can be diagnosed from telemetry.
when: Building any feature that will run in production
Adding a new service, endpoint, background job, or external integration
A production incident took too long to diagnose
Setting up or reviewing alerting rules
Reviewing a PR that adds I/O, retries, queues, or cross-service calls
notWhen: Diagnosing a failure happening right now — use debugging-and-error-recovery instead
Profiling and optimizing measured slowness — use performance-optimization instead
Launch-day monitoring checklists and rollback triggers — that is shipping-and-launch
You cannot name 2-4 on-call questions the telemetry must answer, so you would just log everything
example: "/make-it-observable, we're shipping the payment retry" → the agent first writes the 2-4 questions on-call will ask.

gate.what: Instrumentation only. It halts if you cannot name the on-call questions, but that is a readiness bar, not an approval.

name: simplify-this-code
summary: Simplifies code for clarity without changing behavior, one tested change at a time, following project conventions and scoping to recently modified code.
when: Refactoring for readability without changing behavior
Code works but is harder to maintain than it should be
Reviewing code that accumulated unnecessary complexity
A proposed simplification would only move the difficulty somewhere else
Deep nesting, long functions, nested ternaries, generic names or duplicated logic need cleanup
You are about to simplify code whose original purpose you do not yet understand
notWhen: You are also adding a feature or fixing a bug in the same change; refactors must be separate PRs
The simplification requires modifying tests to pass, which means behavior changed
The code is outside the scope of the current task and you were not asked to broaden scope
You cannot answer what the code is responsible for, what calls it, or why it exists (Chesterton's Fence)
example: "Simplify this function" → the agent checks git blame, callers and the defining tests, then makes one change and runs the suite.

gate.what: No destructive action is gated; it reverts a change when tests fail rather than asking for approval.

name: write-the-docs
summary: Authors documentation a cold reader can act on: gather context, agree the outline before prose, reader-test, then link it from an entry point.
when: The user asks to write or rewrite a piece of documentation
Drafting a proposal, technical spec, decision record, RFC, README section, or PR description
Before shipping a feature that adds user-facing behavior and needs doc updates
A document must be understandable without this session's context
Writing anything that lives under docs/, mintlify-docs/, or gitbook/
notWhen: GSD template-scaffolded artifacts (M###-CONTEXT.md, S##-SUMMARY.md, DECISIONS.md, KNOWLEDGE.md), which are out of scope by design
Producing a spec that drives implementation, which needs the spec gates
A quick summary of what was done in this conversation rather than a document for a reader
example: "/write-the-docs document the auth flow for new contributors" → the agent first names the reader and the single action they must be able to take.

gate.what: It shows the outline to the user and offers a cold-reader subagent, but gates no destructive action.

name: diagram-the-system
summary: Creates validated architecture, workflow, sequence, dataflow, lifecycle, ERD, class, tree, timeline and waterfall diagrams as standalone interactive HTML, plus one-page explainers; code-backed diagrams trace repository evidence.
when: A system, API call chain, pipeline, schema, state machine, class model, tree, timeline or waterfall needs a diagram
A repository or design needs an architecture map grounded in files and commits
A decision, comparison or diagnosis would land better as a one-page explainer
A PR, handoff or document needs a visual that a reader can open without the tool
notWhen: The user wants a dashboard or a live data visualization rather than a static system diagram
The request is a freehand illustration or decorative image, not a technical diagram
There is no Node.js 18+ or browser available for the browser gate; use a text explanation instead
example: "Map the request path from the browser through the API and cache to PostgreSQL" -> a sequence or architecture diagram with source cards and a validated HTML artifact.

gate.what: No approval gate. finalize runs validate, check and browser gates, and a non-zero exit is not success.

name: deslop-the-writing
summary: Scans text for AI-writing fingerprints, rewrites by meaning, re-scans until clean, then checks the register fits its genre.
when: User says deslop, deslopify, or remove the AI tells
Draft has "not X but Y" contrasts, em-dash density, or rule-of-three lists
Text reads uniformly cadenced, puffery-laden, or hedged both ways
Before publishing any agent-drafted prose
The text must fit a genre: academic, tweet, reddit, email, blog, docs, marketing
notWhen: Facts or claims are wrong — this is a style pass; flag, do not silently fix
You want manufactured voice: fake typos, forced slang, humanizer-tool output
Precision-critical academic or technical text where adding attitude makes it worse
example: "Deslopify this blog post" → the agent confirms genre and the claim, runs the tell scan, and reports a findings table before rewriting.

gate.what: Style pass only; nothing destructive is gated.

name: ship-it
summary: Verifies tests, detects the git environment and base branch, offers merge, pull request or keep, then commits, pushes and cleans up.
when: Implementation is complete and the full test suite passes
You need to decide between merging locally and opening a pull request
The branch lives in a worktree and cleanup rules must be applied
On a detached HEAD and need the reduced push-as-new-branch menu
You want the base branch confirmed before merging
Pre-commit hygiene: staged-diff check, secrets grep, tests, lint, typecheck
notWhen: Tests are failing: the skill reports the failures and stops, it does not fix them
You want to discard the work: that path exists only on an explicit human request, never as a menu option
The push was rejected: investigate; force-push only on explicit request
A worktree holds uncommitted files only it has: removal is refused, never force it on your own initiative
example: "/ship-it" → the agent runs the full suite, detects the git environment and base branch, then presents the merge/PR/keep menu.

gate.what: It waits for the human's menu choice before merging or pushing, and permanent deletion of a branch and worktree needs the human to type "discard".

name: guard-the-dangerous-stuff
summary: Hand-applied checklist before destructive commands: recursive deletes, DROP/TRUNCATE, force-push, reset --hard, kubectl delete, docker prune, and PowerShell equivalents.
when: Before rm -rf, DROP TABLE/DATABASE, TRUNCATE, force-push or git reset --hard
Before any command that can destroy data, uncommitted work or production state
Before kubectl delete, docker rm -f or docker system prune
Before PowerShell/cmd equivalents: ri -r -fo, rd /s, Clear-Disk, irm | iex
Before the destructive contract step of a migration
notWhen: Deleting node_modules, dist, .next, __pycache__, build, coverage or .turbo — listed as safe exceptions
Read-only inspection, builds or ordinary test runs
You expect an automatic intercept — the upstream hook is not installed, this is a written procedure only
Deciding whether to deprecate a system at all — that is a product call, answered by the deprecation questions
example: "/guard-the-dangerous-stuff I'm about to git push --force" → the agent checks the pattern table, confirms it targets a non-default branch, and asks for separate authorization.

gate.what: Destructive steps must be made explicit and separately authorized (recursive delete, DROP/TRUNCATE, force-push, reset --hard, kubectl delete, docker prune); HIGH-tier shapes are hard-denied.

name: write-a-new-skill
summary: Writes and refines SKILL.md files: frontmatter, context pointers, information hierarchy and progressive disclosure, leading words, pruning, plus TDD pressure-testing of skill wording.
when: Authoring a new skill
Improving an existing skill
A skill keeps being ignored or misapplied
A skill description or pointer does not reliably trigger when its material is needed
A skill document is sprawling and needs reference pushed behind pointers
Closing the rationalizations found when agents run the skill
notWhen: Writing human-facing prose docs, READMEs, RFCs or proposals: that is a document for a fresh reader, not an agent-consumed skill
Writing a spec or plan before code
You only need to find and invoke an existing skill
example: "/write-a-new-skill I want a skill that stops agents skipping tests" → the agent first runs the pressure scenario without the skill and records the baseline.

gate.what: It requires baseline and post-skill test runs, but no human approval gate.

name: set-the-quality-bar
summary: Turns a project's quality bar into a written CONSTRAINTS.md with numbers and tools, then guards the diff against quietly weakened checks.
when: Starting a project or feature and no quality bar is written down
The user says "set up constraints", "define our standards" or "add quality gates"
An agent is producing volume nobody reads line by line
CI has checks but nobody knows which ones block a merge
Coverage, performance or accessibility numbers get re-argued per PR
About to run an autonomous loop where only the agent-written test suite stands before main
notWhen: The project already has CONSTRAINTS.md and the user is not changing it; read and follow it instead
One-off scripts, spikes or throwaway prototypes
The user wants a code review now (code-review-and-quality) or a CI pipeline built (ci-cd-and-automation)
Non-interactive contexts such as CI, /loop or autonomous runs: the interview needs a live user
example: "Set up quality gates for this repo" → the agent reads package.json, lint and CI config, reports what it found in two lines, then asks Q1.

gate.what: Nothing destructive is gated; it does stop for a four-question interview with a live user.

name: split-across-agents
summary: Runs independent tasks in parallel subagents with focused, self-contained prompts, then reviews, integrates and runs the full suite on what returns.
when: 3+ test files fail with different root causes
Multiple subsystems are broken independently
Each problem can be understood without context from the others
No shared state between investigations
A large job can be dispatched instead of done inline
Each dispatched agent can get one scope, one goal, constraints and an expected output
notWhen: Failures are related, so fixing one might fix others; investigate together first
Understanding the problem requires seeing the full system state
Exploratory debugging where you do not yet know what is broken
Agents would interfere by editing the same files or using the same resources
example: "/split-across-agents" → the agent groups the failures into independent domains and dispatches one focused subagent per domain in one response.

gate.what: No destructive action is gated; returned work goes through a review-and-integrate gate instead.

name: hand-off-to-next-session
summary: Writes a tight continue.md in the active slice and refreshes STATE.md and summaries so a fresh session resumes in one minute.
when: User says pause, hand off, bookmark this, or I'll come back later
Context budget is running low mid-task
Before a risky operation such as a dependency upgrade or major refactor
End of a long multi-day session with unfinished work
notWhen: The work is finished — a slice summary is the artifact, not a handoff
You want a chat recap of the journey — the next agent doesn't need it
Nothing is in flight and no concrete next action exists
example: "/hand-off-to-next-session I'm out of context" → the agent writes the last action, one concrete next action, and what not to do into continue.md.

gate.what: It updates summaries, cancels or waits for background jobs, and stops cleanly without an approval gate.

name: watch-my-context
summary: Installs a per-turn canary line (name, turn counter, self-check) so context degradation shows immediately, and runs a checkpoint-and-re-anchor recovery protocol when it trips.
when: Starting a long or high-stakes session and wanting an early-warning signal
The user mentions a canary, context canary, or canary check
The user notices the canary stopped appearing and asks what happened
The agent can no longer find the canary contract in its own context
The user asks how trustworthy the current context still is
notWhen: You want a check that survives compaction across all sessions: a standing canary in CLAUDE.md or agent memory measures only file-based instruction attention, a weaker signal
You want structural assurance that harder constraints (architecture decisions, never-touch rules) still hold; a present canary is only weak evidence of health
You expect a positive canary to prove context is fine; the test is one-sided and only a missing canary is strong evidence
example: "/watch-my-context" → the agent states the contract "Julius · t1 · ctx ok" and prefixes every later reply with it.

gate.what: It recommends a fresh session and asks the user's name if unknown, but gates no destructive action.
